title: Statistical Analysis Graphs: A Checkable Visual Language for Bayesian Analyses
content: Whether a statistical analysis can be trusted often depends on what its methods section describes least clearly: what was known when each forecast was made, which data were used for fitting and which for scoring, which decisions were made after the outcomes were seen, and which results rest on a check that failed. We present statistical analysis graphs, a visual language for Bayesian analyses in which these facts are drawn and checked. Fifteen elements distinguish quantities by role and relations by kind, separate an event from the time it became known, and separate a posterior from its numerical approximation. One translation rule gives every diagram an exact mathematical meaning, and a validator reports what is wrong, missing or impossible to check, without filling anything in. The translation works in both directions: a sufficiently specified methods section can be written as a compact SAG figure, for a paper, poster or slide, and the figure can be read back into conventional prose and mathematics. Five real analyses and four probes could all be expressed in the language. In three blinded studies, AI readers given only the language reference recovered most of the intended findings. Applied to a preprinted rolling-origin forecasting study of the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak, the validator traced twenty-five findings to five problems and stated what the study would need to record for its forecasts to count as prospective, and the figure could be read back, line by line, into the study's methods statements.
